meta.description: TrekLink handsets pass position, status and SOS to each other over a LoRa mesh, with no cell tower, and sync every event to your basecamp gateway when an uplink returns.

problem.heading: On a multi-day route, the phones go quiet for days
problem.without.label: Without a mesh
problem.with.label: With TrekLink
problem.a.without: A fall is found when someone walks back to look.
problem.a.with: The carrier's node asks, then raises the alarm where it happened.
problem.b.without: Nobody can say where the group is.
problem.b.with: Position hops between handsets, so the group tracks itself.
problem.c.without: Basecamp hears what happened after you walk out.
problem.c.with: Basecamp gets every queued event once one node reaches the gateway.
how.heading: From a press on the ridge to a responder at camp
how.diagram.label: A terrain map with a mesh of trekker nodes, one guide's node and a basecamp station. An SOS from one node ripples outward through every link until it reaches the station.
how.a.title: Raise it
how.a.body: Press the SOS button on v1 or v2. On v3 and v4, hold the button for three seconds.
how.b.title: It spreads
how.b.body: Every node in range repeats it, so it ripples through the group and around any gap.
how.c.title: Basecamp sees it
how.c.body: The station syncs it to the operations system the moment it arrives.
nodes.heading: Four iterations, one firmware
nodes.lede: Each version fixed what the last one taught us. All four run the same TrekLink mesh firmware, set per board at build time.
nodes.carousel.label: Node versions
node.v1.name: v1
node.v1.body: A perfboard build that proved mesh, GPS and fall detection work together. Mesh only, with no cloud uplink.
node.v1.alt: TrekLink v1 prototype in a grey enclosure with a small OLED screen and a square SOS button
node.v2.name: v2
node.v2.body: The first purpose-built board and the first with a compass. Syncs to the cloud over MQTT.
node.v2.alt: TrekLink v2 in its enclosure, with a blue-framed OLED screen and a round metal button
node.v3.name: v3
node.v3.body: A LilyGO T-Beam with GPS on board. SOS is a deliberate three-second hold, so a pocket can't send one.
node.v3.fall: No, the board has no motion sensor
node.v3.alt: TrekLink v3 in a slim ribbed case with a small screen and an antenna
node.v4.name: v4
node.v4.body: The pocket-safe hold from v3, with fall detection back, a real-time clock and a microSD slot.
node.v4.alt: TrekLink v4 in a slim ribbed case with a centred screen and an antenna
board.heading: A board designed for the route

board.alt: The assembled TrekLink v2 circuit board with its ESP32-S3, LoRa radio and GPS modules
faq.heading: Before you pack it
faq.a.q: What if no one is in range when I press SOS?
faq.a.a: The node keeps the SOS and sends it as soon as another node or the basecamp gateway comes into range.
faq.b.q: Do we need a SIM, a phone plan or internet on the route?
faq.b.a: No. Handsets talk to each other directly over LoRa. Only the basecamp gateway needs an uplink, and only to sync.
faq.c.q: Which radio band does it use?
faq.c.a: Nodes default to the MY_433 region, 433.0 to 435.0 MHz, the band set for Vietnam and Malaysia.
cta.heading: Watch your group's events arrive at basecamp
cta.body: The operations system shows every event the mesh syncs from the route.

mesh.heading: Open source at the core, field-tested by a worldwide community
mesh.body: TrekLink's firmware builds on Meshtastic, the open-source LoRa mesh project started in 2020. The radio layer is public code with a large community behind it. TrekLink adds the safety layer on top.
mesh.add.a: Store and forward: an event raised in a dead zone waits on the node and delivers in order.
mesh.add.b: Fall detection that asks the carrier before it alarms, on v1, v2 and v4.
mesh.add.c: An SOS that stays open until a responder closes it, even after the buzzer is silenced.
